To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
anti‐galactosyl‐ceramide autoantibodies in patients with nervous stage African trypanosomiases recognize an antigen common to different strains and located on the membrane of trypanosomes.

anti‐galactosylceramide (anti‐GalC) antibodies cross‐react with a trypanosome proteolipid and this cross‐reactivity is likely to be the cause of the neurological disorder associated with the nervous stage of human African tryparosomiasis.

anti‐Galactocerebrose (GalC) auto‐antibodies are detected in the serum and CSF of HAT patients and that these antibodies cross‐react with a proteolipid of T. brucei which is common to different strains.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immune response in the nervous phase of HAT.
the study of the pathogenic mechanisms involved in human African trypanosome infections.
the pathophysiology of the neurological manifestations of human African try panosomiasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anti‐galactosyl‐ceramide (GalC) autoantibodies detected in CSF from HATS patients are induced by molecular mimic of GalC with the parasite membrane antigen, a 52kD proteolipoprotein.
anti‐Gal‐C antibodies detected in HAT patients might result from molecular mimicry with the parasite antigen.
anti‐Gal C antibodies are produced in response to infection by trypanosomes and that they cross‐react with GalC, a myelin component.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GalC‐like molecules are expressed by trypanosomes and may be responsible for the induction of anti‐GalC autoantibodies in HAT patients.
the parasite antigen recognized by anti‐GalC autoantibodies might be a pathogenetic factor for the nervous stage of HAT.
the anti‐GalC antibody is a pathogenic factor in the nervous form of HAT, and that the anti‐proteolipid antibody is an auto‐antibody.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nervous phase of African trypanosomiase is characterized by a demyelinating process, with the appearance of anti‐GalC autoantibodies in the CSF.
anti-GalC antibodies in HAT patients might result from a cross-reaction with a parasite antigen.
anti‐Galactocerebrose (GalC) autoantibodies cross‐react with an antigen located on parasite membrane.
